model_output.verdict: A computer science graduate with software projects and an internship that leaves the work too general.
write_up: This is pretty common, and it won't stand out in a pile. A recruiter sees a 2026 computer science graduate with a software engineering internship and hands-on projects. The hesitation is that the internship lines don't say which features, tests or fixes were yours, or what changed. Let's start there.

The Personal Finance Tracker line is your model: it names what you built, what it does and the tools you used. Move Experience above Education, then bring that same detail to your internship and help desk work.

cards.line: Motivated and detail-oriented Computer Science graduate seeking a Software Engineer position where I can leverage my technical skills and passion for problem solving to contribute to a dynamic team.
cards.cannot_tell: A recruiter can see the job you want, but the adjectives don't distinguish your work. Keep the Software Engineer target and put your internship work in its place.
cards.example: Computer Science graduate seeking a Software Engineer position, with experience developing [features] for an internal inventory management web application using React and Spring Boot
cards.question: Which inventory application features did you develop during your internship?

cards.line: Education sits above Experience.
cards.cannot_tell: Your help desk and internship work give a recruiter more to look at than coursework alone. Put Experience above Education so that work comes first.
cards.question: Can you move Experience above Education?

cards.line: Soft Skills: Communication, Teamwork, Leadership, Time Management, Problem Solving
cards.cannot_tell: These skills are broad enough to fit almost any applicant. Your soccer captain role gives you a place to show leadership through something you did instead.
cards.example: Intramural Soccer Team Captain, 2023 - 2025: [what you organized]
cards.question: What did you organize as soccer team captain?

cards.line: - Responsible for developing features for an internal inventory management web application using React and Spring Boot
cards.cannot_tell: The application and tools are named, but the features aren't. A recruiter needs to know what you developed.
cards.example: Developed [features] for an internal inventory management web application using React and Spring Boot
cards.question: Which features did you develop for the inventory application?

cards.line: - Participated in daily stand-ups and sprint planning meetings as part of an Agile team
cards.cannot_tell: The meetings are clear, but what you contributed in them isn't. If there was a useful contribution beyond attending, name it; otherwise, make room for your development work.
cards.example: Participated in daily stand-ups and sprint planning meetings as part of an Agile team, sharing [contribution]
cards.question: What did you contribute to stand-ups or sprint planning?

cards.line: - Wrote unit tests to improve code quality and reliability
cards.cannot_tell: A recruiter can't tell which code you tested or what the tests checked. The stated aim is useful, but the tests themselves would tell more.
cards.example: Wrote unit tests for [code or feature] to check [behavior]
cards.question: Which code did you test, and what behavior did the tests check?

cards.line: - Collaborated with cross-functional teams to gather requirements and deliver solutions
cards.cannot_tell: This doesn't say which teams you worked with or what requirements you gathered. Name a solution and your part in getting it delivered.
cards.example: Collaborated with [teams] to gather requirements for [solution] and [your contribution to delivery]
cards.question: Which teams did you work with, and what did you contribute to a solution?

cards.line: - Fixed bugs and performed code reviews
cards.cannot_tell: Both are useful engineering work, but a recruiter can't tell what you fixed or reviewed. One concrete example would make the work count.
cards.example: Fixed [bug] and reviewed [code or feature]
cards.question: What is one bug you fixed and one piece of code or feature you reviewed?

cards.line: - Provided technical support to students and faculty for hardware and software issues
cards.cannot_tell: The people you supported are clear, but the issues aren't. Name the kinds of problems you handled.
cards.example: Provided technical support to students and faculty for [hardware issues] and [software issues]
cards.question: What hardware and software issues did you commonly handle?

cards.line: - Resolved tickets in a timely manner and documented solutions
cards.cannot_tell: A recruiter can't tell how many tickets you handled or what you documented. A typical workload and an example solution would give the job more substance.
cards.example: Resolved [number] tickets per [time period] and documented solutions for [issue]
cards.question: How many tickets did you typically resolve, and what is one solution you documented?

cards.line: - Assisted with setting up laptops and classroom technology
cards.cannot_tell: The equipment is named, but your part in setting it up isn't. Keep the assistance at its real size and say what you handled.
cards.example: Assisted with setting up laptops and classroom technology by [your task]
cards.question: What tasks did you handle when assisting with those setups?

cards.line: - Built a Python application to track expenses and visualize spending with matplotlib
cards.cannot_tell: Keep this as a model. The action and purpose sit together, so a recruiter doesn't have to guess what the application is for.

fit.note: Your internship and projects point toward entry-level software engineering work. The React and Spring Boot internship and full-stack capstone are especially relevant, but the internship needs more detail about your contributions.
